thread.title: Alabama Prepares to Execute Jeffery Lee by Lethal Injection Amid Legal Battle Over Method
thread.title_full: Alabama Prepares to Execute Jeffery Lee by Lethal Injection Amid Legal Battle Over Method

author: Mynorthwest
title: Alabama Prepares to Execute Jeffery Lee by Lethal Injection Amid Legal Battle Over Method
text:
Alabama is set to execute Jeffery Lee, a death row inmate convicted in a 1998 pawn shop murder, by lethal injection on Thursday evening after a judge barred the use of nitrogen gas. Lee's case highlights controversies surrounding judicial override, the legality of switching execution methods, and the state's broader use of nitrogen and lethal injection. His supporters argue the state breached an agreement to use nitrogen, while the attorney general's office insists the switch to lethal injection is lawful. The Supreme Court petition to halt the execution reflects ongoing national debates over execution protocols.
Alabama is preparing to carry out the execution of Jeffery Lee on Thursday evening at 6 p.m. by lethal injection at the William C. Holman Correctional Facility in south Alabama, following a court order that prevented the state from using nitrogen gas as the method of execution.
Lee, who is 49 years old, was found guilty of capital murder for the killings that occurred during a 1998 pawn shop robbery in the rural Dallas County town of Orrville. He has been on death row for nearly 28 years, a period during which his case has drawn attention to the contentious issue of judicial override and the methods states can use to execute convicted murderers.
The incident that led to Lee's conviction took place on December 12, 1998, at Jimmy's Pawn Shop. Shop owners Jimmy Ellis, an Elvis impersonator known by the stage name Orion, and Elaine Thompson were shot to death by Lee when he returned to the shop after claiming he needed money from his grandmother. A third employee survived by feigning death and called 911.
Witness testimony confirmed that Lee entered the shop, demanding to see wedding rings before returning with a sawed‑off shotgun and opening fire. Ellis and Thompson were killed instantly, and another employee was gravely injured but survived. The brutality of the crime and the high profile of Ellis as a former national performer amplified the public outcry that followed.
In 2017 Alabama legislated the abolition of judicial override in capital cases, meaning that juries' sentencing recommendations should no longer be superseded by trial judges. However, this change was not made retroactive, leaving a cohort of death row inmates, including Lee, who had been sentenced to death even though their juries had recommended life without parole. The jury that convicted Lee had voted 7‑5 for a life sentence but the judge, under the old law, imposed a death penalty.
Lee's legal team has long maintained that the state's earlier use of nitrogen as a potential execution method, and the agreement Lee signed to relinquish his right to a lethal injection, should bind the state to the nitrogen protocol. Yet the Alabama attorney general's office proceeded to file new paperwork to change the method to lethal injection, prompting the state's defense lawyers to file a petition with the U.S. Supreme Court seeking a stay of execution.
The lawsuit argues that the state's agreement with Lee was a binding promise that it would execute him only by nitrogen hypoxia if at all. Lee's attorneys claim that reversing to lethal injection violates that agreement and is therefore unconstitutional. Their argument also suggests that the state could revise the nitrogen protocol to meet constitutional standards or adopt other methods such as a firing squad.
In contrast, the attorney general's office argues that there is no legal impediment to switching methods and that the state must proceed with the execution to uphold the rule of law and avoid further delays that continue to inflict harm on the victims' families and the state's legal system. The Supreme Court has not yet ruled on the petition, leaving the execution date in limbo, although the prosecutor's office has urged the high court to allow the execution to proceed.
The case also reflects broader trends across the United States. More than 26 executions have taken place nationwide in 2026, including a lethal injection of a Texas inmate convicted of a triple murder at a neighbor's home.
Meanwhile, Georgia's court blocked an execution of a man who killed two real estate agents. In Alabama, lethal injection remains the primary method, but since 2024 the state has also experimented with nitrogen gas, a method that involves replacing breathable air with an inert gas through a respirator mask. Nitrogen has now been used in seven Alabama executions and once in Louisiana.
The public debate over the morality and legality of different execution methods continues, especially as states face challenges in procuring and administering lethal injection drugs. Supporters of Lee have organized campaigns such as the "HONOR THE JURY" rally outside the Alabama Capitol, demanding that the jury's recommendation of life imprisonment be respected.
They argue that the state's actions undermine the integrity of the criminal justice system and that the use of nitrogen as a nominal threat has been manipulated to sidestep the will of a jury. Lee himself has filed a lawsuit in 2016 contesting the state's lethal injection protocol and in 2018 dismissed that lawsuit in exchange for a promise that he could be executed only by nitrogen if necessary.
The current legal battle centers on whether that promise can be breached or if the state can switch to lethal injection after the fact. The impending execution has raised numerous ethical and legal questions about the state's obligations, the rights of the condemned, and the role of judicial oversight.
As the nation watches, Alabama's decision on how and when to carry out Lee's death penalty will likely influence future debates over execution methods, judicial override, and the treatment of death row inmates across the United States
